latin: Arma virumque cano, Troiae qui primus ab oris Italiam, fato profugus, Laviniaque venit litora.
english: I sing of arms and the man who first, exiled by fate, came from the shores of Troy to Italy and the Lavinian coast.
context: The poem's opening invocation, announcing Aeneas's fated journey from ruin toward a new home.
reading: As an answer to "{question}" — the lot opens at the very beginning of the story: a departure forced by circumstance, not choice, that nonetheless leads somewhere new. Whatever you're facing may be less a single event and more the start of a longer journey whose shape you can't yet see.

latin: Tantaene animis caelestibus irae?
english: Can there be such anger in heavenly minds?
context: The narrator marvels at Juno's relentless wrath against Aeneas, wondering how the divine can hold such a grudge.
reading: Applied to "{question}" — this line points at anger, perhaps not your own, that seems out of proportion to its cause. It suggests looking at whether resentment (yours or someone else's) is driving events more than reason is.

latin: Tantae molis erat Romanam condere gentem.
english: So great a labor it was to found the Roman race.
context: The narrator's aside after cataloguing all the suffering Aeneas endured before Rome could exist.
reading: On "{question}" — the verse suggests that what you're building or attempting is simply heavy by nature, not because you're doing it wrong. Difficulty here may be proof of scale, not a sign to quit.

latin: O passi graviora, dabit deus his quoque finem.
english: O you who have suffered worse than this, god will grant an end to this too.
context: Aeneas rallying his storm-battered crew, reminding them they have survived worse.
reading: As an answer to "{question}" — the lot counsels perspective: you have gotten through harder things than this before, and this too will end. It leans toward endurance rather than drastic action.

latin: Forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit.
english: Perhaps someday it will be a pleasure to remember even this.
context: Aeneas again, encouraging his men mid-crisis — the single most quoted line of the poem.
reading: For "{question}" — the oracle answers with distance rather than certainty: whatever this is, imagine looking back on it later. If the thought of that vantage brings relief, proceed; if it brings dread, that itself is telling.

latin: Durate, et vosmet rebus servate secundis.
english: Endure, and save yourselves for better things to come.
context: The close of Aeneas's speech to his men after the storm.
reading: On "{question}" — a straightforward answer: hold on. The lot advises patience and self-preservation now, on the premise that conditions will improve and you'll want to still be standing when they do.

latin: Sunt lacrimae rerum et mentem mortalia tangunt.
english: These are the tears of things, and mortal matters touch the mind.
context: Aeneas weeping before a mural of the Trojan War, moved that even strangers know his people's suffering.
reading: Answering "{question}" — the verse doesn't offer a plan, only permission to grieve. If your question carries loss, the lot suggests the feeling itself deserves acknowledgment before any decision does.

latin: Quidquid id est, timeo Danaos et dona ferentis.
english: Whatever it is, I fear Greeks — even bearing gifts.
context: Laocoon's warning against the Trojan Horse, ignored at Troy's cost.
reading: For "{question}" — a caution: something on offer may not be what it appears. The lot suggests distrusting whatever looks too convenient or too generously given, whatever its source.

latin: Una salus victis nullam sperare salutem.
english: The one safety for the conquered is to hope for no safety.
context: Aeneas, in the burning ruins of Troy, urging his last companions into a fight they cannot win.
reading: As an answer to "{question}" — a hard reading: sometimes the only way through is to stop calculating the odds of safety and act anyway. Fitting if you've been waiting for a guarantee that isn't coming.

latin: Dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat?
english: Trickery or courage — who asks, against an enemy?
context: Aeneas justifying his men's use of disguise and deception in battle.
reading: On "{question}" — the lot suggests the method matters less than you think, if the cause is just. It may be permission to use an indirect or clever approach rather than a purely honorable one.

latin: Quid non mortalia pectora cogis, auri sacra fames?
english: To what do you not drive human hearts, accursed hunger for gold?
context: The narrator's condemnation of Polydorus's murder, killed for the gold he carried.
reading: For "{question}" — a warning about motive. If money or gain sits anywhere near your question, the oracle asks you to look hard at whether it's quietly distorting the choice.

latin: Anna soror, quae me suspensam insomnia terrent!
english: Anna, my sister, what dreams keep me in dreadful suspense!
context: Dido confiding in her sister the anxiety and longing that will undo her.
reading: Answering "{question}" — the lot names anxiety itself as the subject. It may be worth telling someone what's actually keeping you up, rather than deciding alone in the dark.

latin: Fama, malum qua non aliud velocius ullum.
english: Rumor, than which no other evil is swifter.
context: The introduction of Fama (Rumor) as she spreads word of Dido and Aeneas across Africa.
reading: On "{question}" — beware what others will say, and how fast. The oracle suggests reputation or gossip may be moving faster than the truth of the matter, and shouldn't be mistaken for it.

latin: Varium et mutabile semper femina.
english: A fickle and changeable thing, ever, is woman.
context: Mercury's dismissive line to Aeneas, urging him to distrust Dido's constancy and leave — the poem's most notorious editorializing, voiced by a god with his own agenda.
reading: For "{question}" — read this one skeptically, as the ancients themselves often did: it's a warning about someone else's constancy, spoken by a messenger with a motive of his own. The lot may be less about them than about who's telling you to distrust them, and why.

latin: Vixi, et quem dederat cursum Fortuna peregi.
english: I have lived, and I have finished the course that Fortune gave me.
context: Dido's last words before her death, looking back on her life as complete.
reading: As an answer to "{question}" — a note of closure. The lot suggests this chapter is finished, whatever comes next, and that there's dignity in calling it complete rather than fighting to extend it.

latin: Possunt quia posse videntur.
english: They can, because they believe they can.
context: The narrator, on the crew of Cloanthus pulling ahead in the ship race through sheer belief.
reading: On "{question}" — a vote of confidence. The lot suggests the main obstacle may be your own belief in the outcome, and that conviction itself will move things forward.

latin: Tu ne cede malis, sed contra audentior ito.
english: Do not yield to misfortunes, but go against them all the more boldly.
context: The Sibyl of Cumae, prophesying more trials ahead for Aeneas — and telling him to meet them head-on.
reading: For "{question}" — direct counsel to press forward rather than retreat. The lot reads the situation as one that rewards boldness, not caution.

latin: Facilis descensus Averno... sed revocare gradum superasque evadere ad auras, hoc opus, hic labor est.
english: The descent to hell is easy... but to retrace your steps and escape to the air above, that is the task, that is the labor.
context: The Sibyl warning Aeneas how easy it is to enter the underworld, and how hard to leave it.
reading: As an answer to "{question}" — a caution about entry versus exit. Getting into this situation may have been effortless; the oracle warns that getting back out will be the real work, so plan for that now.

latin: Tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento... parcere subiectis et debellare superbos.
english: Remember, Roman, to rule the peoples with authority... to spare the humbled and war down the proud.
context: Anchises, in the underworld, describing Rome's future mission to his son Aeneas.
reading: For "{question}" — the lot advises a double standard applied on purpose: mercy toward those who yield, firmness toward those who don't. Consider whether you're applying the same approach to everyone when the situation calls for two.

latin: Flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo.
english: If I cannot bend the gods above, I will stir up hell itself.
context: Juno, thwarted by the other gods, resolving to work through darker means instead.
reading: On "{question}" — a warning about escalation. If the direct, respectable route isn't working, the lot notes that someone (maybe you) may be tempted toward a less scrupulous one. Worth asking whether that's wisdom or just frustration talking.

latin: Aude, hospes, contemnere opes et te quoque dignum finge deo.
english: Dare, guest, to scorn riches, and make yourself too worthy of a god.
context: Evander, welcoming Aeneas into his humble home, urging him not to judge by wealth.
reading: As an answer to "{question}" — the lot suggests measuring this by something other than money or appearances. Worth may lie in the offer itself, however modest, rather than in its price.

latin: Me, me, adsum qui feci, in me convertite ferrum.
english: Me, me — I am the one who did it, turn your blades on me.
context: Nisus, trying to take the blame and the killing blow to save his friend Euryalus.
reading: For "{question}" — the lot raises the question of who should bear the cost here, and suggests that stepping forward yourself, rather than letting someone else absorb it, may be the answer.

latin: Fortunati ambo!... nulla dies umquam memori vos eximet aevo.
english: Fortunate pair!... no day will ever erase you from the memory of time.
context: The narrator's tribute to Nisus and Euryalus after their deaths, sealing their friendship in verse.
reading: On "{question}" — the lot points toward what will be remembered rather than what will be immediately gained. If this involves someone else, the bond itself may matter more, and outlast, whatever the outcome.

latin: Audentis Fortuna iuvat.
english: Fortune favors the bold.
context: Turnus, rallying his side as battle is about to begin.
reading: As an answer to "{question}" — a push toward action. The lot favors the bolder of your options, spoken as it is by a side about to charge rather than one waiting to be attacked.

latin: Stat sua cuique dies... sed famam extendere factis, hoc virtutis opus.
english: Each has his own appointed day... but to extend one's fame through deeds, that is the work of courage.
context: Jupiter, unable to save Pallas from his fated death, noting that what remains within anyone's control is how they act, not how long they live.
reading: For "{question}" — the lot separates what's fixed from what's not. Outcomes and timing may be out of your hands; what you do in the meantime isn't. Focus there.

latin: Nescia mens hominum fati sortisque futurae.
english: The mind of man knows nothing of fate or what's still to come.
context: The narrator's comment on Turnus, gloating over a kill without knowing his own death is already near.
reading: On "{question}" — a note of humility: whatever you're currently confident about, the lot reminds you that none of us can actually see what's coming. Hold the certainty loosely.

latin: Experto credite.
english: Trust one who has been through it.
context: Diomedes, a veteran of the Trojan War, warning Latin envoys against provoking Aeneas — advice earned the hard way.
reading: As an answer to "{question}" — the lot points you toward someone who has already lived through something like this, and suggests their word is worth more here than fresh theorizing, including your own.

latin: Disce, puer, virtutem ex me verumque laborem, fortunam ex aliis.
english: Learn courage from me, boy, and true hard work; learn luck from others.
context: Aeneas arming for the final duel, advising his young son Ascanius.
reading: For "{question}" — the lot separates what can be taught from what can't. Effort and character are things you can pass on or build yourself; luck isn't, so don't wait on it.

latin: ...vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras.
english: ...and his life fled with a groan, resentful, down to the shades.
context: The poem's final line: Aeneas kills Turnus, and the Aeneid ends abruptly, without resolution or relief.
reading: On "{question}" — the lot lands on an unresolved, uneasy ending, not a triumphant one. Even a decisive act here may not bring the closure or peace you're hoping for. Reading this doesn't mean don't act — it means don't expect the ending to feel clean.
